<ConflictType> — Evidence shows both substantial job losses predicted by some studies and no detectable employment reductions reported by others

Researchers disagree sharply: multiple high-credibility studies (e.g., Neumark & Shirley; CBO) predict job losses from minimum wage hikes, while UC Berkeley’s Reich and coauthors find no decline in employment and even reduced vacancies. Some papers emphasize short-run stability but long-run job growth reductions, while others claim no discernible effect on unemployment. These mutually exclusive outcomes reflect differences in scope, methods, and time horizons rather than mere detail variations.

The minimum wage’s effect on jobs is actively contested in the literature. On one side, widely cited analyses report that higher minimum wages reduce employment, especially for teens and less-educated workers [d1], and large-scale federal hikes are predicted to eliminate over a million jobs [d7,d10,d11]. On the other side, UC Berkeley’s research finds no job losses and argues that higher wages reduce turnover and job vacancies rather than total jobs [d3,d4,d9]. Some studies even suggest short-term employment may be unchanged even as long-run job growth slows [d5]. Because these findings are mutually exclusive within the same national context and time frame, the evidence reflects Conflicting opinions and research outcomes.
